\item \added{\textbf{Geographic Transferability:} Our study area-northern Finland's boreal zone-features relatively flat to gently undulating terrain (typical slopes $<$5\textdegree), homogeneous boreal forest land cover, and predominantly dry continental snow. These conditions represent a favorable scenario for SAR-based fusion: gentle topography minimizes SAR geometric distortions (layover, foreshortening, radar shadow), and dry snow exhibits relatively stable C-band backscatter characteristics \cite{ulaby1986microwave, nagler2000improved}. Consequently, our reported performance metrics should be interpreted as achievable under near-optimal SAR acquisition geometry, and transferability to other geographic and climatic settings cannot be assumed without dedicated validation. \\

In complex alpine terrain (e.g., European Alps, Himalayas, Andes), three interacting factors would present substantial challenges. \textit{First}, SAR geometric distortions scale nonlinearly with terrain slope relative to the radar look angle. At Sentinel-1's nominal incidence angles (29\textdegree--46\textdegree), foreslopes exceeding approximately 20\textdegree\ produce severe foreshortening where topographic relief is compressed in the range direction, while slopes approaching the complement of the incidence angle cause layover, where returns from multiple elevations collapse into the same range cell, rendering affected pixels physically uninterpretable \cite{tsai2019remote}. Radar shadow on steep back-slopes creates complete signal voids. Critically, these distortions concentrate in high-altitude accumulation zones where accurate snow monitoring is most needed for downstream water resource forecasting \cite{immerzeel2010large}. \textit{Second}, snow metamorphism varies substantially across climatic regimes, producing fundamentally different SAR-optical signatures. Maritime snowpacks (e.g., Scandinavian coast, Cascades) are warm, dense, and undergo frequent melt--freeze cycles that cause strong C-band absorption through liquid water content \cite{nagler2016advancements}; continental interior snowpacks (e.g., Rocky Mountains, Siberia) remain cold and dry with depth hoar and faceted grain growth exhibiting volume scattering; and transitional regimes (e.g., Himalayan basins) display complex diurnal melt--refreeze stratification varying with elevation \cite{snapir2019spatiotemporal}. Feature representations learned from northern Finland's predominantly dry boreal snow may therefore not generalize to regimes where SAR-snow interactions are governed by different physical mechanisms. \textit{Third}, the strong coupling between elevation, aspect, solar illumination geometry, and snow distribution in mountainous terrain creates spatial heterogeneity at scales far finer than observed in our study area, where snow distribution is governed primarily by vegetation canopy density and latitude rather than topographic position. \\  Several architectural properties of XFuse are relevant to these challenges, though their effectiveness in alpine settings remains unvalidated. The bidirectional cross-attention mechanism enables each modality to selectively attend to the other through learned query-key-value projections-in SAR-degraded regions, the attention weights could theoretically shift toward optical spectral features, analogous to the mechanism's designed behavior under cloud contamination but operating in the reverse direction. The quality-aware training framework, which learns continuous sample weighting from heterogeneous metadata, provides a natural extension point: terrain-derived quality indicators (local incidence angle, layover/shadow masks from DEM analysis) could be incorporated as additional metadata channels, enabling systematic down-weighting of geometrically distorted SAR observations. However, these remain architectural affordances rather than validated capabilities. \\  Robust geographic generalization would require: (1) radiometric terrain correction of Sentinel-1 data using high-resolution DEMs to mitigate slope-dependent radiometric biases; (2) incorporation of topographic variables (slope, aspect, curvature, sky view factor) as auxiliary model inputs through a dedicated terrain encoder path; (3) training on geographically diverse datasets spanning boreal, alpine, and maritime snow regimes to capture regime-dependent SAR-optical relationships; and (4) domain adaptation or transfer learning strategies to efficiently extend learned representations to undersampled snow climate zones. We consider multi-region validation across contrasting terrain types and snow climate regimes as the primary direction for extending this work toward globally applicable operational deployment.}

Consequently, our reported performance metrics should be interpreted as achievable under near-optimal SAR acquisition geometry, and transferability to other geographic and climatic settings cannot be assumed without dedicated validation. \\

Radar shadow on steep back-slopes creates complete signal voids. Critically, these distortions concentrate in high-altitude accumulation zones where accurate snow monitoring is most needed for downstream water resource forecasting \cite{immerzeel2010large}. \textit{Second}, snow metamorphism varies substantially across climatic regimes, producing fundamentally different SAR-optical signatures. Maritime snowpacks (e.g., Scandinavian coast, Cascades) are warm, dense, and undergo frequent melt--freeze cycles that cause strong C-band absorption through liquid water content \cite{nagler2016advancements}; continental interior snowpacks (e.g., Rocky Mountains, Siberia) remain cold and dry with depth hoar and faceted grain growth exhibiting volume scattering; and transitional regimes (e.g., Himalayan basins) display complex diurnal melt--refreeze stratification varying with elevation \cite{snapir2019spatiotemporal}. Feature representations learned from northern Finland's predominantly dry boreal snow may therefore not generalize to regimes where SAR-snow interactions are governed by different physical mechanisms. \textit{Third}, the strong coupling between elevation, aspect, solar illumination geometry, and snow distribution in mountainous terrain creates spatial heterogeneity at scales far finer than observed in our study area, where snow distribution is governed primarily by vegetation canopy density and latitude rather than topographic position. \\  Several architectural properties of XFuse are relevant to these challenges, though their effectiveness in alpine settings remains unvalidated. The bidirectional cross-attention mechanism enables each modality to selectively attend to the other through learned query-key-value projections-in SAR-degraded regions, the attention weights could theoretically shift toward optical spectral features, analogous to the mechanism's designed behavior under cloud contamination but operating in the reverse direction. The quality-aware training framework, which learns continuous sample weighting from heterogeneous metadata, provides a natural extension point: terrain-derived quality indicators (local incidence angle, layover/shadow masks from DEM analysis) could be incorporated as additional metadata channels, enabling systematic down-weighting of geometrically distorted SAR observations. However, these remain architectural affordances rather than validated capabilities. \\  Robust geographic generalization would require: (1) radiometric terrain correction of Sentinel-1 data using high-resolution DEMs to mitigate slope-dependent radiometric biases; (2) incorporation of topographic variables (slope, aspect, curvature, sky view factor) as auxiliary model inputs through a dedicated terrain encoder path; (3) training on geographically diverse datasets spanning boreal, alpine, and maritime snow regimes to capture regime-dependent SAR-optical relationships; and (4) domain adaptation or transfer learning strategies to efficiently extend learned representations to undersampled snow climate zones. We consider multi-region validation across contrasting terrain types and snow climate regimes as the primary direction for extending this work toward globally applicable operational deployment.}

message.content: QC abbrvation is a quality control or what

content.text:
Yes — **QC = Quality Control** in this context.

In the GFSC (Copernicus CLMS HRWSI) product, the `QC` and `QCFLAGS` layers are per-pixel quality control bands that indicate:

- **QC**: Overall quality indicator (e.g., cloud-free, cloud-filled, interpolated, no data)
- **QCFLAGS**: Bit-flag layer encoding specific quality conditions (sensor geometry, algorithm confidence, cloud shadow, etc.)

In the manuscript they appear as `QC\,+\,QCFLAGS` in the dataset table (line 41 of `4_Result.tex`), and in the training pipeline they're used as quality weights in the loss function:

```
weight = (confidence^α) × (quality_mask^β)
```

where `quality_mask` is derived from these QC layers to down-weight unreliable pixels during training.

However, transformers' quadratic computational complexity and requirement for extensive training data limit their applicability to high-resolution satellite imagery. Hybrid CNN-Transformer architectures represent the current frontier, synergistically combining CNNs' efficient local feature extraction with transformers' global contextual modeling. Recent research demonstrates the effectiveness of hybrid CNN-Transformer architectures for remote sensing applications, particularly in change detection tasks. EHCTNet represents a strategic approach that combines CNNs for multi-scale feature extraction with transformer blocks for global reasoning, addressing limitations in existing frameworks that struggle with missed detections and discontinuity issues \citep{yang2025enhanced}. The architecture employs dual-branch feature extraction modules and enhanced token mining based on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks to improve semantic information derivation \citep{yang2025enhanced}. RCTNet further advances this paradigm by introducing early fusion backbones and Cross-Stage Aggregation modules for enhanced temporal representation, demonstrating superior performance over traditional methods while maintaining optimal balance between accuracy and computational cost \citep{gao2024relating}. However, multiscale fusion introduces computational trade-offs that require careful consideration. Research shows that while hybrid models can achieve high accuracy (97.97\% on field images), fusion benefits are context-dependent and may not always justify the 15\% increase in FLOPs, particularly for edge deployment scenarios \cite{njoroge2024multiscale}.

Full CNN-Transformer hybrids have shown particular promise for glacier and snow-related mapping, extending to snow cover due to overlapping challenges in ice-snow differentiation. \citet{maslov2025globally} presented GlaViTU, a scalable hybrid convolutional-Transformer model for glacier delineation from multimodal satellite data (optical, SAR, and DEM), achieving expert-level accuracy in debris-covered regions by fusing local CNN details with Transformer's global context. Although focused on glaciers, its applicability to snow mapping is evident in handling complex terrains, as corroborated by similar architectures in avalanche monitoring \cite{bianchi2025monitoring}, where deep learning on SAR data segments snow events with high precision. Furthermore, \citet{wang2021loveda} explored MaxViT, a multi-axis vision Transformer hybrid, for snow cover in forested mountains using Sentinel-2, yielding Dice scores up to 0.928 and demonstrating robustness to acquisition variability via transfer learning. Hybrid models incorporating moisture elimination and temporal dynamics have further advanced SWE forecasting. \citet{xu2022hybrid} leveraged moisture-aware preprocessing with hybrid deep learning for enhanced evaporation and snowmelt predictions, while \citet{tarricone2023estimating} integrated lag-time snow depth data into advanced machine learning pipelines, improving predictive accuracy in remote sensing-ground data fusion. These approaches underscore the need for multimodal inputs where machine learning on L-band products from airborne campaigns achieved reliable mappings in alpine areas. Despite these strides, persistent limitations include cloud-snow confusion, data scarcity for training, and computational demands of Transformers \citep{zhang2024efficient, li2025multi}. Future directions may involve State Space Models (as in recent change detection hybrids \cite{dong2024conmamba}) or further physics-deep learning integration to enhance real-time applicability. 


Ma \etal \cite{ma2024multilevel} proposed FTransUNet, a multilevel multimodal fusion scheme for semantic segmentation of urban remote sensing scenes. Their architecture combines CNN-based shallow-level feature fusion through Squeeze-and-Excitation modules with a three-stage Fusion Vision Transformer (FVit) for deep-level feature fusion. The FVit alternates between self-attention layers for intra-modal feature enhancement and Adaptively Mutually Boosted Attention (Ada-MBA) layers that perform simultaneous self-attention and cross-attention to fuse VIS imagery with DSM height data. Evaluated on ISPRS Vaihingen and Potsdam datasets, FTransUNet achieved 92.40\% overall accuracy and 84.23\% mIoU for urban scene classification (buildings, trees, roads, cars). While FTransUNet demonstrates effective multilevel fusion for urban scenes, its design reflects several assumptions specific to classification tasks with uniform-resolution inputs that limit applicability to broader remote sensing challenges. First, the architecture requires \textit{all inputs at identical spatial resolution}, VIS and DSM data are preprocessed to matching dimensions before processing. This constraint fails to address the fundamental multi-resolution characteristics of operational satellite constellations where Sentinel-1 (10m), Sentinel-2 optical bands (10-60m), and reference datasets (often $\geq$60m) exhibit inherent resolution heterogeneity. Second, FTransUNet targets \textit{discrete semantic classes} through cross-entropy optimization, lacking mechanisms for continuous-valued regression tasks prevalent in earth observation (fractional snow cover, vegetation indices, soil moisture). The classification-focused design employs hard decision boundaries inappropriate for phenomena exhibiting gradual spatial transitions. Third, the architecture provides \textit{no quality-aware learning mechanisms}, all training samples receive equal weighting despite variable data quality from atmospheric conditions, sensor artifacts, and annotation uncertainty that systematically affect operational satellite data streams. Fourth, FTransUNet lacks \textit{uncertainty quantification}, providing point predictions without confidence estimates essential for operational decision-making in critical applications. Most critically, FTransUNet's fusion strategy operates at \textit{fixed spatial scales} determined by input resolution, lacking adaptive mechanisms for multi-resolution processing. The architecture cannot train on coarse-resolution labels while leveraging fine-scale input information, nor can it generate high-resolution predictions that exceed training target resolution, fundamental capabilities required when reference data availability constrains achievable output resolution. These limitations motivate our approach: CrossFuse extends the multilevel fusion paradigm to address heterogeneous-resolution inputs, continuous-valued prediction tasks, quality-aware learning, and uncertainty quantification while preserving FTransUNet's core insight that explicit cross-modal attention mechanisms significantly outperform simple concatenation strategies.

Quality-aware learning has emerged as essential for handling the inherent uncertainties in snow cover estimation, where annotation noise, sensor artifacts, and environmental variability challenge conventional supervised learning. Recent work on uncertainty quantification in remote sensing reveals that explicit uncertainty modeling improves not only prediction accuracy but also provides crucial confidence metrics for operational hydrology applications \citep{braverman2021post, povey2015uncertainty}. Methods range from simple ensemble variance to sophisticated decompositions of different uncertainty sources, though practical implementations often focus on total uncertainty for operational efficiency. The integration of quality flags and metadata, such as Theia Snow's multi-class confidence scores, into the learning process through attention-weighted loss functions reduces the impact of mislabeled training data by up to 25\% \citep{gascoin2019theia}. Furthermore, robust training techniques including Co-teaching strategies and dynamic loss decay mechanisms specifically designed for remote sensing have shown remarkable resilience to label noise rates exceeding 30\%, common in crowd-sourced snow cover annotations \citep{lin2024robust}. Multi-resolution fusion presents unique challenges beyond simple data integration, requiring architectures that preserve fine-scale spatial detail while leveraging coarse-resolution temporal consistency. Traditional approaches using fixed fusion strategies fail to adapt to varying snow conditions and sensor quality. Recent adaptive fusion methods employing learnable gating mechanisms dynamically weight contributions from different resolutions based on local image statistics and temporal context, achieving superior performance particularly in forest-snow boundaries where resolution matters most \citep{li2022deep, meraner2020cloud}. The incorporation of attention mechanisms, both channel-wise for feature selection and spatial for regional focus, enables models to automatically identify and prioritize the most informative resolution for each spatial location, a capability particularly valuable when fusing Sentinel-1's 20m SAR with Sentinel-2's variable 10-60m multispectral bands \citep{khan2021effect}. Despite these advances, critical gaps remain that motivate our proposed approach. Existing fusion methods typically employ static architectures that cannot adapt to varying data quality and availability. Current models lack explicit mechanisms for handling the multi-resolution nature of operational satellite constellations, often defaulting to simple resampling that destroys valuable scale-specific information. Most significantly, few existing architectures jointly optimize for pixel-level accuracy and physically-consistent spatial patterns while providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

This work explores whether a quality-aware hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture combining adaptive multi-resolution fusion, hierarchical processing that preserves scale-specific features, and spatial regularization can provide accurate snow cover fraction estimates with calibrated uncertainty. We demonstrate proof-of-concept capabilities on Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 image pairs with diverse snow coverage scenarios (0.2\%-75.5\%), achieving 89.52\% accuracy with excellent calibration (ECE=0.025). While these results are promising, comprehensive comparative evaluation against operational baselines (MODIS, VIIRS VNP10, traditional NDSI approaches), multi-regional assessment across diverse geographic and climatic conditions, and temporal validation remain essential future work for establishing operational readiness and assessing practical advantages over existing methods.
